query: Earlier refractory high-entropy alloys illustrate persistent trade-offs: MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW retained good yield strength from 600 to 1600 °C, with MoNbTaVW reaching 842 MPa at 1000 °C, but both had poor room-temperature fracture toughness and high density; HfNbTaTiZr showed room-temperature ductility above 50% and a yield strength of 929 MPa but only 295 MPa at 1000 °C; and as-cast HfMoTaTiZr achieved about 1600 MPa at room temperature and 855 MPa at elevated temperature but retained a density of 10.21 g cm−3. Given the constraint that density must be reduced without sacrificing the strong room- and high-temperature mechanical performance of as-cast HfMoTaTiZr, what single intervention should be tested? Provide a mechanistic hypothesis, predicted outcomes relative to the as-cast baseline, explicit temperature and loading boundary conditions, supporting evidence from the preceding RHEA results, and a controlled experiment with quantitative rejection criteria that could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partially substituting about 20 atomic percent of Hf with aluminum (Al) in the as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy will reduce its density by roughly 15% while sustaining its high room‐temperature and elevated‐temperature yield strengths.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐cast equiatomic HfMoTaTiZr, which exhibits a single‐phase BCC structure, a density of approximately 10.21 g/cm³, a room‐temperature yield strength near 1600 MPa, and an elevated‐temperature yield strength close to 855 MPa.
generation.intervention: Replace roughly 20 at.% of Hf with Al, forming a modified alloy (nominal composition Al_xMoTaTiZr, where x is selected to substitute one‐fifth of the previously Hf content) while keeping the other constituent elements unchanged.
generation.conditions: Perform compressive mechanical tests at room temperature and at 1000 °C under comparable strain‐rate conditions to those in the baseline experiments.
generation.structural_mediator: Retention of a primarily single‐phase BCC solid solution with minimal—or at least benign—secondary phase formation that could detrimentally affect ductility or high‐temperature strength.
generation.mechanism: Al has a much lower atomic mass than Hf and is known from lightweight RHEA studies to lower alloy density. Its addition will induce additional lattice distortion that compensates for the loss of heavy Hf in terms of solid–solution strengthening. This strategy leverages findings in Al‐containing lightweight RHEAs, suggesting that a similar mechanism can maintain high yield strengths at both room and elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: The alloy’s density is expected to decrease to approximately 8.5–9 g/cm³ (a ~15% reduction) while preserving a room‐temperature yield strength near 1600 MPa and an elevated‐temperature yield strength around 850 MPa, with fracture toughness and ductility remaining acceptable.
generation.baseline: The as‐cast HfMoTaTiZr alloy with 10.21 g/cm³ density, ~1600 MPa yield strength at room temperature, and ~855 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.boundary: Study limited to as‐cast microstructures (i.e., without additional homogenization or thermal treatments beyond casting) and test under compressive loading at room temperature and 1000 °C; the intervention is confined to a single substitution (Hf → Al) without adding additional alloying elements.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal extends lightweight alloy strategies from Al‐containing RHEAs (e.g., as reported in PMC8074761 and PMC8746096) to the heavy Hf–based system (PMC7514121). However, the phase stability upon Hf substitution and any risk of deleterious Al‐rich precipitates are not yet demonstrated in HfMoTaTiZr, introducing uncertainty regarding microstructural evolution and ductility maintenance.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize an as‐cast alloy where approximately 20 at.% of Hf in HfMoTaTiZr is substituted with Al. Verify phase formation and homogeneity via XRD and SEM/EPMA. Then, perform compressive tests at room temperature and at 1000 °C using standard strain rates, and measure density via Archimedes method.
measurements: Phase identification and lattice parameters via XRD
Room-temperature compressive yield strength and fracture strain
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy’s density is reduced by less than 10% compared to 10.21 g/cm³ or if the yield strength at room temperature or at 1000 °C deteriorates by more than 10% relative to the baseline values, the hypothesis will be falsified.

He defined high-entropy alloys (HEAs) as having five or more major elements beneath 5–35 at.%, and minor elements below five at.%. In 2006, he also established four core effects of HEAs []: High-entropy, severe-lattices-distortion, sluggish-diffusion, and the cocktail effect. With the new concepts, scientists are able to develop and expand alloys without restrictions [,,,,]. Some HEAs have been found to have attractive properties on diffusion [], oxidation [], corrosion [], fatigue [], creep [], fracture toughness [], and elevated-temperature strength []. AbstractSingle-phase solid-solution refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) have been receiving significant attention due to their excellent mechanical properties and phase stability at elevated temperatures. Recently, many studies have been reported regarding the precipitation-enhanced alloy design strategy to further improve the mechanical properties of RHEAs at elevated temperatures. In this study, we attempted to develop precipitation-hardened light-weight RHEAs via addition of Ni or Co into Al0.8NbTiV HEA. The added elements were selected due to their smaller atomic radius and larger mixing enthalpy, which is known to stimulate the formation of precipitates. The addition of the Ni or Co leads to the formation of the sigma precipitates with homogeneous distribution. The formation and homogeneous distribution of sigma particles plays a critical role in improvement of yield strength. Furthermore, the Al0.8NbTiVM0.2 (M = Co, Ni) HEAs show excellent specific yield strength compared to single-phase AlNbTiV and NbTiVZr RHEA alloys and conventional Ni-based superalloy (Inconel 718) at elevated temperatures.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory alloys, lightweight, sigma phase, mech

Adding lightweight elements into RHEAs can effectively reduce the density and improve the specific strength [,,,]. For example, Senkov et al. fabricated Al0.4Hf0.6NbTaTiZr RHEA by adding Al into the HfNbTaTiZr RHEA. The density of the alloy decreased from 9.94 to 9.05 g/cm3, and the specific yield strength increased from 93.56 to 203.43 MPa∙cm3/g []. However, their plasticity deteriorated significantly. Recently, Yang et al. found that NbTiVTaAl0.25 RHEA with Al addition still have outstanding compressive plasticity greater than 50% []. Nevertheless, the specific strength of this alloy is only 151.48 MPa∙cm3/g, which has the potential for further improvement. In this work, a series of lightweight TaNbVTi-based RHEAs were fabricated by mechanical alloying (MA) followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS). The microstructural evolution and its effects on mechanical properties were analyzed.
